Teach & Think — 40 min

Props, characters & genre iconography

Read this section carefully before you start the annotation task.

Mise-en-scène is a French term meaning "placing on stage." In Media Studies, it means everything the director or designer deliberately puts in front of the camera (or, for a poster, within the frame): props, costume, setting, lighting, and where characters are positioned. Nothing in a poster is accidental.

When certain props, settings and character types are used over and over again across a genre, until audiences instantly recognise the genre just from seeing them, we call this iconography.

Props

Weapons, masks, blood — objects that signal danger or violence.

Characters

Killers, victims, survivors — recognisable character types.

Setting

Forests, abandoned buildings, darkness — isolating locations.

Theorist Claude Lévi-Strauss argued that stories create meaning through binary oppositions — pairs of opposite ideas or characters placed in tension with each other, such as:

Hero vs. Villain
The protector figure set against the threat.
Safety vs. Danger
A calm, ordinary world disrupted by threat.
Civilisation vs. Wilderness
The familiar, controlled world against the unknown.

Why this matters for GCSE: spotting iconography and binary oppositions lets you explain how a genre is constructed, not just describe what's in the image — this is exactly what Section A of your exam rewards.

Enrichment — not required for your exam

Vladimir Propp studied hundreds of traditional stories and found the same character roles kept appearing. Three useful ones to know:

Hero — the character who resolves the danger. Villain — the character who creates the danger. Helper — a character who assists the hero.

This isn't a theorist named in your Eduqas specification, but it's a useful lens for thinking about "who's who" in a poster — feel free to use it in your annotations if it helps, but you won't be tested on Propp's name in the exam.

Worked example: 30 Days of Night (2007)

Here's iconography and binary opposition applied to one poster, modelled for you.

Props & iconography

The axe and gun are weapon iconography — signalling this is a fight for survival. The blood-red colour wash is a horror colour convention signalling danger and violence.

Characters

Two ordinary-looking survivors, not professional fighters — their positioning (man in front, woman behind) suggests a protector/protected character dynamic.

Setting

An implied snowy, isolated town (referenced in the title) — isolation iconography common in survival horror.

Binary opposition

Safety vs. danger: ordinary people (safety, the familiar) forced into violence (danger, the threat) — the poster doesn't show the monster, but implies its presence through the characters' fear and weapons.

Propp role (enrichment)

The man could be read as a Hero figure (resolving danger); the unseen threat implied off-poster is the Villain.

Your turn: Friday the 13th (2009)

Now apply the same method independently. Do this in your OneNote page — paste the poster image below and annotate it directly using the leading questions.

Annotate in OneNote — leading questions

  1. Props: Identify at least two props or objects in the poster. What genre do they signal, and how do you know?
  2. Characters: Describe the character shown. What type of character do they appear to be, and what visual clues tell you this?
  3. Setting: What kind of location is implied? Why is this setting typical of horror iconography?
  4. Binary opposition: Identify one binary opposition at work in this poster (e.g. safety vs. danger, civilisation vs. wilderness). Explain how the poster creates this contrast.
  5. Optional — Propp role: If you were to assign a Propp character role to the masked figure, which would it be, and why?

Stretch: apply it again

Finished early? Repeat the method on one or both of these posters in OneNote.

Annotate in OneNote — same five questions

  1. Props: Identify at least two props or objects. What genre do they signal?
  2. Characters: Describe the character type shown and the visual clues that tell you this.
  3. Setting: What kind of location is implied, and why is it typical horror iconography?
  4. Binary opposition: Identify one binary opposition and explain how the poster creates it.
  5. Optional — Propp role: Assign a Propp character role to one figure in the poster, and justify your choice.

In your OneNote page, write:
